title: The Empress Seizes Power
tagline: She overthrew her husband, took the throne, and ruled Russia for 34 years.

scenes.text: St. Petersburg, June 28, 1762. A German princess named Sophie — who has lived in Russia since age 14 and remade herself into more Russian than the Russians — puts on a military uniform, rides at the head of the Preobrazhensky Guards, and deposes her own husband from the throne of Russia.

scenes.speaker: Catherine the Great
scenes.text: Peter was a tsar who despised Russia, mocked the Orthodox Church, and insulted the army that protected him. I love Russia. I have spent my life learning its language, its faith, its history. If one of us should rule it, let it be me.

challenge.instruction: Peterhof, before dawn: Alexei Orlov has ridden through the night with a note from the Guards. Read the grid code — it tells Catherine whether this is the morning she takes Russia.
challenge.fact: In July 1762, Catherine organized a coup against her husband Tsar Peter III — who was widely seen as weak and pro-Prussian. The Imperial Guard supported her; Peter was arrested and died days later (likely murdered). Catherine ruled Russia for 34 years as Catherine II.

scenes.text: Catherine ruled for 34 years — longer than any other Russian monarch. She corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, commissioned translations of the Encyclopédie, founded the Hermitage Museum, established the Smolny Institute for the education of women, and expanded Russia's borders to encompass 200,000 additional square miles.

scenes.speaker: Voltaire
scenes.text: Your Majesty writes to me of legal reform, of education, of the abolition of torture. Europe's monarchs have not gone so far. What inspires you?

challenge.fact: Catherine ruled Russia for 34 years — longer than any other female ruler in Russian history. She expanded Russia's territory by 520,000 square kilometres and corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot while suppressing the very freedoms they championed.
challenge.instruction: Catherine writes to Voltaire of reform, but Russia lives on its harvest. Plan the village fields the way her Free Economic Society urges — rye, oats, clover and fallow — so there is grain to sell and fodder for the herd.

scenes.speaker: Catherine the Great
scenes.text: Russia is a vast country that has been asleep. I intend to wake it without breaking it. Enlightenment cannot be imposed on serfs at bayonet point — it must be grown from the top down, school by school, law by law. I am patient. A country this large rewards patience.

challenge.instruction: To wake Russia, Catherine backs the self-taught genius Ivan Kulibin. Build his single timber arch across the Neva, every strut pushing, so it can carry its load without a pier in the ice-choked river.
challenge.fact: In 1769 Catherine made Ivan Kulibin, a self-taught clockmaker from Nizhny Novgorod, head of the mechanical workshop of the Academy of Sciences. Besides his Neva bridge he built a searchlight with mirrors, a river boat that winched itself upstream, and mechanical legs for wounded soldiers.

scenes.text: Catherine's contradictions were enormous: she wrote eloquently about liberty while owning millions of serfs. She corresponded with philosophers about human rights while crushing the Pugachev Rebellion with brutal force. She was the Enlightenment's greatest patron and, in some ways, its most revealing hypocrite.

challenge.instruction: Catherine's coup is underway. Promise what each Guard regiment and power in Petersburg wants — without driving the others away — before Peter III realises what is happening.
challenge.fact: On 28 June 1762 (9 July in the modern calendar) Catherine rode from Peterhof to the barracks of the Izmailovsky Guards, then the Semyonovsky and Preobrazhensky, and by mid-morning was proclaimed empress at the Kazan Cathedral in St Petersburg. Peter III, who had alienated the army by making peace with Prussia, signed his abdication the next day.

scenes.speaker: Catherine the Great
scenes.text: I am accused of contradiction. Very well. I rule the largest country on earth with a borrowed philosophy and an army of advisors who disagree with each other. A ruler who is never contradicted is a ruler who is no longer listening. I would rather be a contradiction than a tyrant who never questions herself.

challenge.fact: Catherine bought whole collections at once — Gotzkowsky's 225 paintings in 1764, Count Brühl's in 1769, Crozat's in 1772, Walpole's in 1779 — and wrote that it was not love of art but greed. Her Hermitage opened to the public in 1852 and today holds over three million objects.
challenge.instruction: Catherine retreats to her 'hermitage' beside the Winter Palace, where the pictures she buys by the hundred wait to be hung. Place each masterpiece in the room that shows it best.

scenes.speaker: Catherine the Great
scenes.text: Two face-down cards: one at Amsterdam, one at St Petersburg. We cannot see who they are until we attack, and an attack reveals every card at the location. The Coup already runs at Amsterdam; you hold a card to start one at St Petersburg.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 5 · Face Down. Win two attacks: fight at Amsterdam where the Coup is running, then carry the fight to St Petersburg by starting your own event there.
challenge.fact: A card on the board can be public (face up) or private (face down). A private card hides its identity and stats from rivals until an attack reveals every card at that location. Your own cards deploy face down; Toggle Public when being seen helps you.
